sections.section_title: Paul's Boasting and the Corinthians' Readiness
sections.summary: Paul explains that he has boasted to the Macedonians about the Corinthians' readiness to participate in the collection for the Jerusalem saints, using reciprocal motivation between the churches.

sections.section_title: The Practical Urgency — Sending Brothers Ahead
sections.summary: Paul sends delegates ahead to ensure the collection is arranged in advance as a willing gift (eulogia) rather than an exaction (pleonexia), protecting Paul's credibility and the quality of the Corinthians' giving.

Paul applies the agricultural metaphor of sowing and reaping to generous giving, insisting that each person must give as he has decided in his heart — not reluctantly or under compulsion — because God loves a cheerful giver.
sections.relevance: The passage establishes that human choices produce corresponding consequences — generous sowing yields an abundant harvest of righteousness, stingy sowing a meager one. The neutral reading connects this to the same sowing/reaping structure in Galatians 6:7-9, which explicitly ties the direction of sowing to eternal life versus corruption. Verse 7 emphasizes free human decision as essential to God-pleasing action: each person must choose deliberately in the heart, not under external compulsion. This presupposes genuine human agency whose choices produce real outcomes, a framework incompatible with unilateral divine determination of results.
key_phrases: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly
whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully
each one must give as he has decided in his heart

sections.section_title: God's Ability to Supply and the Psalm of the Righteous Giver
sections.summary: Paul declares that God is able to make all grace abound so the Corinthians may have sufficiency for themselves and overflow into good works, then cites Psalm 112:9, which identifies the righteous person's generous distribution to the poor as the righteousness that endures forever.
sections.relevance: The passage presents a cooperative divine-human model: God provides enabling grace and sufficiency, but the purpose is that humans 'may abound in every good work' — human action is the intended outcome of divine provision, not a predetermined inevitability. The neutral reading notes that the Corinthians are 'not the terminus of grace but its conduit,' and that the Psalm 112 citation identifies the righteous person's giving as the righteousness itself. The reading states that 'generosity converts temporary resources into permanent righteousness,' implying that human choices produce eschatologically enduring results. This framework presupposes genuine human agency within divine provision rather than unilateral divine determination.
key_phrases: God is able to make all grace abound to you
so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work
he has distributed freely, he has given to the poor

sections.section_title: God as the Supplier of Seed and the Multiplier of Righteousness
sections.summary: Paul draws on Isaiah 55:10 and Hosea 10:12 to describe God as the one who supplies seed for sowing and bread for food, who will multiply the Corinthians' seed and increase the harvest of their righteousness, enriching them for generosity that produces thanksgiving to God.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading explicitly states that 'human action and divine action are not alternatives; they are the two sides of the same agricultural process — the farmer sows, but God gives the rain and the increase.' This synergistic framework presents God as the provider of resources and the multiplier of results, while humans are genuine agents who must choose to sow. The reading also distinguishes between 'seed for sowing' (resources intended to be given away) and 'bread' (sustenance for the giver), implying that the giver who recognizes this distinction exercises genuine discernment and choice. The model is incompatible with unilateral divine determination because it requires real human participation to complete the process.
key_phrases: He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing
increase the harvest of your righteousness
you will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way

sections.section_title: The Collection as Confession, Communion, and Glorification
sections.summary: Paul describes the wider effects of the collection: it supplies material needs, produces thanksgiving and glorification of God from the Jerusalem saints, creates mutual longing and prayer between communities, and makes visible the surpassing grace of God upon the Corinthians.

Paul closes the collection argument with a doxological exclamation — 'Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!' — pointing to the entire economy of grace that underlies and enables the human acts of generosity described throughout chapters 8-9.
